The Mechanism of Fieldsfrom the Bost–Connes System

Shao-Wu Hu
Shanghai, China
forest@xindong.com
ORCID: 0009-0009-8300-4691

Abstract

A field is a distribution of background states and correlations formed by the joint evolution of matter and its background. Building on finite joint dynamics in the Bost–Connes state space and established matter identifications, we connect matter formation, maintenance, and motion to source writing, background transfer, and reception. Matter and its accompanying resources form a complete carrier on which maintenance phase, spatial propagation, and field contacts are connected. Auxiliary returns controlled by edge flux and loop exchange produce electromagnetic storage and, in a controlled long-wavelength window, the Maxwell response. Complete mass endpoints and spatial transport give massive short-range propagation and spin–isospin interaction through pion exchange; color-link loop returns give noncommuting field response. A gravitational background affects both matter maintenance phase and spatial exchange. Two-state occupation preparation with complete package reception gives distinct clock and propagation factors and realizes reciprocal clock–rod scales under finite-time error control. Source, resources, matter, and contact energy remain in one joint evolution. A finite construction with directional constraints supplies two accessible positive-frequency radiation modes and reciprocal absorption. Relative electromagnetic calibration, persistent strong-background closure, and the connection between radiation and material readout require further dynamical relations.

Keywords: Bost–Connes system; mechanism of fields; gravitational fields; gauge fields; observational spacetime.

Chapter 1. Definition of Fields

1.1 Introduction

A charged body changes the motion of nearby charges; the gravity of matter deflects freely falling bodies and changes both light propagation and clock readings. These phenomena share a spatial structure: the same matter system responds differently at different positions, while different matter systems at the same position respond according to their respective properties. Comparing these responses reveals the spatial distribution of the interaction. A field describes this distribution and its variation in time.

This paper builds on the Bost–Connes system [1] and its construction of finite state-space dynamics [2]. The Unification of Matter, Forces, and Spacetime [3] connects matter formation, maintenance phase, and spatial motion within complete joint dynamics. Matter maintains itself through continual exchange with the background and interacts with other matter through that shared background. A joint action determines changes in the states of both matter and background, together with the energy and charge balances on each side. Matter that subsequently contacts this background therefore experiences a different action. The influence of one matter system on another thus follows a continuous process: an action at the source changes the background, the background transmits that change, and distant matter responds through its own coupling.

When the source persists, local exchange can maintain a stationary spatial distribution; when the source changes, the background and its action on matter evolve accordingly. Both the static form and the dynamical behavior of a field must be determined from this joint process.

The source, the background, the matter being acted upon, and the apparatus recording them all belong to the same state-space dynamics. The observational spacetime constructed in Dynamics of the Bost–Connes State Space provides a representation of these processes in three spatial dimensions and one temporal dimension [2]. Field positions, times, and observational outcomes use this representation; their physical content is supplied by the actual exchange, propagation, and records.

1.2 Background Quantities of a Field

The persistent evolution of matter depends on the state of the surrounding background. Background components participating in maintenance determine the available action amplitude; components transmitting excitations carry energy, charge, and relative phase; correlations established through exchange determine how different propagation histories combine in subsequent actions. Changes that matter produces in the background affect other matter through these quantities.

Taking the background under a source-free preparation as the reference, we can track changes before and after the action of matter. For a background unit participating in maintenance, let the projector Ni represent the state in which the unit at position i is occupied and unavailable for the maintenance action under consideration. Its mean occupation is ⟨Ni⟩. For coherently transmitted components, the correlation ⟨Bi†Bj⟩ retains amplitudes and relative phases between positions or channels; here Bi is a local transition operator in the exchange being used. These quantities describe aspects of availability and coherent exchange, respectively. The quantities required in a particular description are determined by the actual coupling between matter and background.

Let Ω(t) be the joint state containing matter, background, and the existing auxiliaries and records. Denote by B the background subsystem that carries the interaction under consideration in the actual joint construction. Its reduced state and a local reading over a region U can be written as

ρB(t)=TrB―Ω(t),bO(U,t)=Tr[ρB(t)OU].(1.1)

Here OU is a background observable acting on that region, with regions defined by the actual position degrees of freedom. Correlations across regions are computed using the corresponding joint observables. Correlations already established between background and matter remain in Ω(t) and continue to participate in subsequent evolution. This description accommodates local occupation, relative phase, and the correlations required for propagation.

Spatial positions follow the observational construction of Ref. [2] and correspond to positions in the actual exchange actions [2,3]. The same type of matter may occur at different positions, and the same position may participate in exchanges through different channels. Matter type, background spectral label, and propagation position each retain their own physical meaning. Which units can exchange directly in space is determined by the specific interaction. Both local field quantities and their spatial connections therefore refer to definite objects.

When matter participates in a contact, its maintenance source, work resources, and formation records remain in the complete carrier [3]. Let J be the isometric embedding of the matter representation into that carrier, K^ the actual maintenance and motion action, and P^x its position projector. The corresponding matter generator K and position projector Px satisfy

K^J=JK,P^xJ=JPx.

These relations carry the persistent phase and position of matter. Background writing and package reception below are written in the matter representation, with internal carrier correlations retained by the complete action; newly introduced background units are listed separately. Section D6 of the dynamical supplement connects function readout and position-controlled contact in the two representations.

A uniform reference background makes identical matter experience the same local action everywhere. After a matter source changes part of the background, the available action and exchange states differ from position to position. Propagation develops these differences into a spatial distribution, which constitutes the field.

1.3 Field Formation

A field source arises through actual contact between matter and background. The persistent action of matter depends on the background, and the background receives the influence of matter in that same action. The resulting change may be a change in the occupation of background units, the injection of energy-carrying or charged excitations, or a change in relative phases and correlations between propagating components. The next contact begins from these altered states, allowing the source action to accumulate through successive evolution.

Reference [3] gives a source process that retains newly produced outputs. The local generator of matter acts on a freshly prepared two-state auxiliary, writing its action strength into the auxiliary output. This output then exchanges with the local background unit, while the old output remains in the joint system. Let ξi=⟨Ni⟩−1/2 denote the occupation change relative to an unbiased preparation, and let εi be the probability of executing this complete update. We use ℏ=1. For the generator eigenvalue λi of a fixed source at rest, this realization gives

ξi′=(1−εi)ξi+εibi,bi=12sin(2treadλi).(1.2)

Here tread is the actual interaction duration between source and auxiliary, and λi is the corresponding generator frequency. When the update is executed, the local unit acquires the new occupation produced by the source; otherwise its previous state is retained. Source writing and background replenishment jointly determine the net change in each cycle. As the occupation approaches the value corresponding to the source output, the difference available for further writing decreases. Exchange with the surroundings can carry this bias away, allowing the source to continue producing a net output into the background.

Mass and clock rates are read over the total elapsed duration. For a cycle whose processing intervals preserve relative phase, if maintenance acts for tH during the total duration τ, with rest-frame half-gap μ during the active interval, the observed rest frequency is m=factμ, where fact=tH/τ [3]. Preparation, readout, retrieval, and waiting repeated each cycle contribute to τ; each contact angle uses its actual generator and duration.

Coherent exchange retains another kind of output. During emission, transmission, absorption, and retrieval between matter systems, a component leaving the emitting matter reaches the receiving matter through the same propagation process. The final auxiliary state and propagation phase jointly determine the final amplitude [3]. Retrieval can restore some auxiliaries to their prepared states while leaving phases or correlations in the matter at the two ends. The background description required for a persistent interaction therefore includes components still participating in propagation and return, as well as their correlations with matter.

These actions can all be composed cycle by cycle within the full joint evolution, using a joint description of repeated interactions [4]. If the auxiliary newly added in cycle n is prepared in ηn, and the actual joint unitary action in that cycle is Un, then

Ωn+1=Un(Ωn⊗ηn)Un†.(1.3)

The existing background, matter, and records remain in Ωn; the new auxiliary is prepared according to the specified process. The actual ordering of source action, propagation, and return is contained in Un. Reduction to the background degrees of freedom gives the background state left by the cycle, while reduction to matter gives the change in the source itself. The field source and the matter response thus come from the same joint final state.

A persistent source repeats this process. Whether a field can be maintained, how long it takes to build up, and how long it persists after the source changes are determined by the joint evolution of writing, propagation, replenishment, and return. The preparation maintaining the source state also belongs to this process; the required supply and retrieval are included in the physical balance.

Figure 1.1. Joint evolution of matter and background. Contact with the source changes the background, and local exchange transmits this change to other matter. Back-reaction and return on all sides remain within the same joint state. Nodes and links represent background units and their couplings; the dashed line indicates correlations that must be retained. When retrieval restores an auxiliary to its prepared state, matter may still retain the phase changes, transfers, and correlations produced by the action.

1.4 Field Propagation

A background change produced at the source can affect another position only through actual exchange. A local contact transfers the change to background units coupled to the source. These units subsequently exchange with the background at other positions, or propagate while carrying excitations, and then contact distant matter. Each segment of the action retains its state, phase, and elapsed duration. Successive actions extend a local source into a spatial response.

In the background-update realization of Eq. (1.2), background units subsequently undergo the specified exchanges. If R is the transport matrix for the first moments of occupation, and Dε=diag(εi), the process of updating first and transporting afterward gives [3]

ξn+1=R(I−Dε)ξn+RDεbn.(1.4)

This equation directly connects the source, propagation, and the distribution already formed: the first term transports the retained background bias, and the second transports the bias newly written in the current cycle. After the source action, background returning to the source region enters the next writing step, so the net source output adjusts together with the surrounding distribution. This occupation recurrence follows from the full exchanges and repreparations used here; coherent propagation is calculated from the corresponding amplitudes and correlations in Eq. (1.3).

For a fixed source, if this update converges under the supply boundary conditions, it ultimately forms a stationary distribution at the corresponding phase of the cycle. Local writing, transport, and replenishment still occur in every cycle, with the changes balancing at the end of each cycle. A static field is maintained by ongoing dynamics. When the source changes in time, new outputs enter the same exchange process in succession, and the previous distribution gradually becomes a new one. Field build-up and variation follow from the same evolution.

The spatial form depends on the actual propagation operator and boundary conditions. For example, equally weighted nearest-neighbor exchange in three dimensions gives a discrete harmonic equation outside the source, with a 1/r distribution in its controlled far-field regime [3]. This field profile follows from conservative exchange in three-dimensional space and the corresponding low-wavenumber response. Changing propagation, restoration, or the boundary changes both the spatial distribution and the build-up time. Source strength and spatial field profile are related within one process, while their respective origins remain distinct.

Propagation time accumulates over the complete process: contact, preparation, transport, retrieval, and waiting all contribute to the actual elapsed duration. The number of exchanges needed to cross a region and the duration of each exchange determine the propagation response. The spatial distribution of a stationary field, the arrival of a time-dependent response, and the speed of phase propagation are each read from this actual evolution.

Figure 1.2. Dynamical maintenance of a stationary distribution. A finite chain of thirteen units governed by Eq. (1.4) illustrates the build-up of the distribution. The central source is continually updated, and both ends exchange with an unbiased supply. All curves show occupations at the end of transport in each cycle. In the stationary state, net source writing is exactly balanced by net outflow through the two ends, while exchange continues. These parameters serve only to illustrate the recurrence mechanism. This is a one-dimensional example; the 1/r far field discussed in the text corresponds to three-dimensional propagation.

1.5 Field Action

After a background change reaches a distant position, it enters the evolution of local matter through that matter's existing coupling. Available background states change the amplitude of the persistent action of matter, while transmitted excitations and phases alter exchange through compatible channels. Source matter and receiving matter are thereby connected through the same background. Treating one matter system as a probe means using its response to describe this interaction.

Field action can be determined by comparison with a reference process. Fix the probe preparation, calibration scales, and actual elapsed duration T. Let ρT(s)(T) and ρT(0)(T) denote the probe outputs with the source action under consideration present and with that action switched off, respectively. For a calibrated probe observable OT, the source-induced change is

δ⟨OT⟩=Tr[OT(ρT(s)(T)−ρT(0)(T))].(1.5)

Both outputs are calculated from actual processes containing the source, background, and probe. Choosing position, coherence, or momentum observables gives changes in distribution, changes in phase and visibility, or momentum transfer, respectively. The momentum difference divided by the total elapsed duration of the action gives the mean force relative to the reference process [3]. The mass and charges carried by the probe determine its coupling. When probe properties can be factored out of the response, the remaining spatial and temporal dependence gives the physical quantities of that type of field.

Coherent action can also directly connect phase and motion. When the actual output in the regime considered is described by an effective generator HT=HT,0+δHT, a background change makes matter accumulate a different phase. For a fixed eigenbranch that remains occupied, let δh(t) be the change in its generator eigenvalue. Then

δφ=−∫0Tδh(t)dt,d⟨P⟩dt=i⟨[HT,P]⟩.(1.6)

Here P is a calibrated momentum operator with no explicit time dependence. The first expression gives the dynamical phase accumulated along the actual evolution; the second gives the momentum change caused by the same action. In a continuum position representation, if the generator change takes the form of a local potential energy V(x,t), its contribution to the rate of momentum change is −⟨∇V⟩. At discrete positions, the corresponding commutator is retained. Spatial differences in the field become forces through matter evolution; phase and impulse are different readings of this action.

The probe generally also affects the background. Treating the source as fixed and the probe as passive is a description valid within a regime of the full process. When back-reaction is required, source, background, and probe continue to evolve jointly. Joint conservation relations in the same realization account for energy and charge changes on each side [2]. This balance connects field action to field formation and supplies a basis for the subsequent discussion of time-dependent fields and radiation.

1.6 Field Observation and Definition

Field action leaves records in matter and apparatus. A moving probe changes its position distribution, an interferometer converts relative phase into output differences, and a clock reflects the local rhythm of evolution by comparing successive processes. The corresponding distinctions are stored in the probe and actual auxiliary degrees of freedom and are read out as events according to the recording scheme. Field observation thus occurs within the same state-space dynamics that produces the field.

Actual pointers determine record components [2]; outcome probabilities and conditional final states together describe a measurement instrument [5]. Let Ωout be the joint final state including detection, and let Πr project onto pointer outcome r. Then

pr=Tr[(I⊗Πr)Ωout],∑rpr=1.(1.7)

The probabilities of the different outcomes and their conditional final states are supplied by the same evolution, and the state left after readout continues into subsequent processes. Expressing event positions, times, and calibrated responses in a common 3+1 representation allows probe responses in different regions to be compared. Background propagation histories, the forces acting on matter, and the final events are linked in sequence within this representation.

Each kind of observation retains the background information it requires. Occupation changes the available action amplitude, relative phase affects interference, and correlations between background and matter or between regions affect repeated contacts. Identical local occupations can correspond to different phase responses. A field description therefore retains the states and correlations relevant to the action under study, and a specific apparatus extracts measurable field quantities from them.

A field can accordingly be defined as the distribution of background states and correlations over position and time in an actual interaction; its influence on matter is determined by responses and records within the same evolution. This paper mainly concerns changes produced and maintained by matter sources in a reference background.

Events collected over space and time give statistical field quantities. In an observational regime with stationary responses, finite correlation times, and sufficiently slow field variation, regional averages can stably characterize the local field. Smooth spatial variation further allows discrete relations to be written as continuum field equations. Statistical precision is determined by the actual event history and its correlations, while the spatial approximation depends on the relation between propagation and observation scales. The continuum field description is thereby connected to the underlying discrete process.

Field and force have related but distinct meanings here: a field describes the background state and distribution through which an interaction occurs, while force describes the momentum change of matter under that action.

1.7 Types of Fields

Changes that matter produces in the background affect other matter through different modes of action. Reference [3] establishes the dynamical counterparts of gravity and gauge interactions. We retain these physical objects and develop their field mechanisms through sources, propagation, and responses.

A gravitational field modulates the persistent evolution of matter through the shared background. The source changes background availability; this change propagates to other positions and is received through the complete maintenance action of local matter. Changes in phase, timing, and motion provide readings of gravitational potential, spacetime calibration, and gravitational action. Their spatial distribution follows from the joint source–background response.

Gauge fields connect exchanges between matter systems through compatible channels. Source charges and exchange structure determine the components available for emission, propagation, and reception; relative phases, multichannel correlations, and receiver couplings determine subsequent responses. Electromagnetic, weak, and color interactions are developed through these channels, while nuclear forces are described through collective exchange between composite matter systems.

Chapter 2. Gravitational Fields

A gravitational field changes the rhythm of matter evolution at different positions. A matter source changes the available share of the nearby background, and background exchange transmits this change elsewhere. Local matter continues to accumulate phase through the same maintenance action and therefore acquires position-dependent energy and clock rates. Spatial gradients deflect its motion, while time calibration makes clocks at different positions accumulate different readings. Potential, force, and timing arise from this common response.

Chapter 1 connected source writing, background propagation, and matter response. Here we first construct a static gravitational field using the continual-refreshing process of Ref. [3], adopting the averaged, long-wavelength, and weak-field description of motion already obtained for that process. We then discuss the relation of the spatial length scale to actual propagation, the general transport structure, and the time-dependent response. Time is accumulated over the complete process, and energy and length use the same distant reference. Denote the speed of light in this reference by c0; below we set ℏ=c0=1.

2.1 Gravitational Potential

The phase of matter is determined by the maintenance generator. When background availability decreases, this action weakens, and phase accumulation slows relative to the reference background. For a single two-state resource unit in Chapter 1, the available response is hi=1−Ni, with mean reference response h0=1/2 under the unbiased preparation. Once the source establishes a stationary bias, the mean response and gravitational potential are

h¯i=h0−ξ*,i,Φi=h¯i−h0h0=−2ξ*,i.(2.1)

In the positive-bias source regime used here, the source increases the unavailable share of the background, so ξ*,i>0 and Φi<0. The distant unbiased supply gives Φ→0 and fixes the reference potential. The potential has a concrete physical meaning: it is the change in the local maintenance response relative to the common baseline.

Let m be the rest energy of test matter without source action. Keeping the same activity fraction as the source-free reference, the mean frequency of the maintenance phase changes from m to m(1+Φi), so the rest-energy change is

Vi=mΦi.(2.2)

Matter type enters the potential energy through m, while the spatial variation of the background is described by Φi. Under the same common maintenance modulation, different matter systems read the same potential. They still have their own masses, internal structures, and channel interactions; the gravitational response acts commonly on their persistent evolution.

The occupation–mean-response relation in Eq. (2.1) is exact for this resource realization. Equation (2.2) applies it within the controlled regime of motion in Ref. [3].

2.2 Sources and Spatial Distributions

Net writing at the source in each cycle determines how much bias the background must transport outward. Let ξ+ be the stationary distribution after refreshing and before transport, let c be the selection probability of each internal exchange edge and each supply edge, and let L be the corresponding graph Laplacian. The update of Chapter 1 gives

cLξ+=j,j=Dε(b−ξ*),ξ*=(I−cL)ξ+.(2.3)

Here j is the actual net source. The bias already accumulated in the background enters the next update and reduces the difference still available for source writing. The net source thus depends both on the source itself and on the returning background. Where there is no refreshing outside the source, local exchange only transfers existing bias, and Eq. (2.3) becomes a discrete harmonic equation [6]. Summing over all positions cancels internal exchanges pairwise, equating net source writing with net outflow through the supply boundary. A stationary distribution is maintained by a continuing flow.

For a single source at s, write G=L−1 for the Green kernel with the given supply boundary conditions. With source refreshing probability ε, eliminating the source occupation from Eq. (2.3) gives [3]

js=cεbsc(1−ε)+εGss,ξ*,i=jscGis(i≠s).(2.4)

The kernel Gis gives the response from the source to position i, while Gss enters the source's own feedback. The distant amplitude and local net writing are determined by the same spatial process. The inverse exists under the given boundary conditions when every relevant connected component can reach the supply. A corresponding large-volume limit can then be taken for regions far from the boundary.

Take actual positions on a three-dimensional nearest-neighbor grid with equal step lengths and equal exchange weights in all six directions. Denoting the step length by ℓx, the low-wavenumber part satisfies L≃−ℓx2∇2. In the far region outside the source, the kernel is

Gis≃ℓx4πr,Φ(r)≃−jsℓx4πch01r,r=|xi−xs|.(2.5)

This 1/r dependence follows from the low-wavenumber response of three-dimensional conservative exchange. Source writing fixes the overall amplitude, while propagation in three dimensions fixes the radial decay. Finite lattice spacing, distance to the boundary, and the spatial extent of the source determine departures from the far-field expression. The detailed profile remains calculable from Eq. (2.3).

For a weak source, bs=treadλs+O((treadλs)3). Calibrating λs by the source's own rest energy Ms measured with the same background clock makes net writing proportional to Ms at leading order. For distributions to which the common source calibration applies and for which feedback between sources is negligible, the leading-order continuum description is

∇2Φ=4πGρM,Φ(r)=−GMsr.(2.6)

Here ρM is the mass density of matter sources at rest; the point-source expression applies in their exterior far field. The mass of a composite source is calibrated by the total generator actually maintained, with binding contributions included in the total phase. Replenishment at the source, feedback between neighboring sources, and finite-source corrections remain in the net writing of Eq. (2.3). Source measures for moving matter and freely propagating radiation are discussed in Sections 4.2–4.3.

2.3 Newton's Constant

Newton's constant compares two outputs of the same process: the mass phase accumulated by the source, and the potential energy acquired by distant matter through the source-induced background change. Equation (2.5) directly gives the leading strength of the process used here,

Gdyn(0)=ℓx4πch0limMs→0jsMs.(2.7)

The source-readout duration, exchange selection in each cycle, return feedback, and complete timing all enter this quantity through js/Ms, c, and ℓx. They determine the amplitude of the actual output and cannot be eliminated from the 1/r profile alone.

The common physical units follow the background spectral calibration of Ref. [3]. If Wmet is the effective participation weight of the gravitational process, Cbg is the total squared spectral gradient of the background used, and E0 is the energy unit, then

Emet2Cbg=E02Wmet(logWmet)2,GE=Emet−2.(2.8)

We retain the single physical calibration of Ref. [3]: Gdyn(0)=GE fixes the correspondence between the gravitational process used here and the spectral unit. The common calibrated strength is denoted by G in the field equations. This matches the actual strength to the common energy scale; the details of source and return remain available for computing finite corrections.

At the participation depth and energy unit adopted in Ref. [3], the spectral scale gives GE≃6.70272×10−39GeV−2.

2.4 Matter Motion and Clock Rates

The same maintenance response enters both rest energy and the energy relation for motion. The passive motion realization in Ref. [3] yields a positive-energy branch when the local background varies slowly. In an isotropic long-wavelength, low-speed representation at the same three-dimensional positions, with c0=1, its leading expansion is

E+(x,p)=m+mΦ(x)+|p|22m+⋯.(2.9)

The rest and kinetic terms use the same m. The wave-packet center moves according to spatial phase variations, hence

X˙=pm,p˙=−m∇Φ,X¨=−∇Φ.(2.10)

The test mass cancels from the leading acceleration because the inertial and potential-energy coefficients belong to the same process. For a point source, Φ=−GMs/r increases with r; its negative gradient points toward the source and thus gives attraction. Higher-order motion retains the effects of lattice dispersion, background gradients, and resource fluctuations. Momentum changes in a finite process are calculated from the actual generator of Chapter 1.

Clock rates read the same matter phase. Let A(x) be the ratio of the local clock frequency to that of the distant reference. For the common response above,

A(x)=1+Φ(x),dτloc=A(x)dt.(2.11)

Here τloc is defined by phase counting of the local clock, while t uses the distant reference. Near the source, A<1, so less clock phase accumulates during the same reference duration. Clocks at different positions can be compared by exchanging signals. For static transmission without additional frequency conversion, the local frequencies at emission position e and reception position r satisfy

νrνe=A(xe)A(xr).(2.12)

When a signal travels from a region of lower clock rate to a distant receiver, the receiver reads a lower frequency. Its leading form connects to the weak-field gravitational-redshift relation [7]. Force and redshift thus share the same potential: the former compares phase gradients between neighboring positions, while the latter compares phase accumulation rates at different positions.

Figure 2.1. Gravitational potential, motion, and clock rates. The exterior potential increases with distance, and its negative gradient accelerates slow matter toward the source. The same negative potential lowers the local maintenance frequency, so clocks accumulate less phase than the distant reference. The curve is a normalized illustration of the weak-field far region; its vertical axis does not represent the full nonlinear result near the source.

2.5 Spatial Length Scales and Geometric Representation

Clocks and rods read how the same background affects different actions of matter. Internal maintenance phase determines the local clock rate, whereas spatial exchange determines the propagation principal part. Both must be computed separately from one complete reception process.

Reception uses a newly prepared work package B and the background package Vx at position x; Sx exchanges these complete packages. The accompanying resources of matter remain within the carrier described by J. Write its generator in the matter representation as K, and use the position-controlled swap and return C=∑xPx⊗Sx, with participating-response projector RB. The reception action is HC=C†(K⊗RB)C. For mutually independent package states σB,σx,σy, also independent of the matter input, the local and edge responses are

ax=Tr(Rσx),tyx=Tr(RσxσBσy).(2.13)

These contractions follow from complete package exchange. The ordered three-package product cannot be replaced by a single occupation. With the original matter mass action MfY and motion matrices αi, the coefficients of the conditional mean maintenance and spatial actions are determined by ax and tyx.

An explicit preparation uses a two-state occupation unit as each complete exchanged package, with independent inputs, a common available state |0⟩, R=|0⟩⟨0|, and σi=diag(hi,1−hi). Archived records remain outside the exchanged packages. Then ax=hx and tyx=hBhxhy. If records or other internal degrees of freedom travel with a package, the complete trace must be evaluated again; diagonal occupation alone does not imply this product. The corresponding self-adjoint action for the stated preparation is

H―=MfYh(X)+νhB∑iαih(X)Dih(X).(2.14)

The order hDih retains gradient contributions in a nonuniform background. With M actual independently prepared work arrays, simultaneously coupled with strength 1/M each, the difference between this mean action and the complete reduced output can be controlled over a finite time window. Arrays, records, and preparation have real resource costs; the environment is not reset during evolution. Section D6 gives the error and phase-readout bounds.

The operators Di in Eq. (2.14) describe spatial propagation on the complete carrier. For a loading in which accompanying resources move with matter, physical translation is SXSR, represented as SX on matter [3]. Spatial reception therefore transports matter together with its contact resources, retaining existing records and relative-position relations.

In a locally uniform, long-wavelength window of nonzero availability, maintenance and propagation share the active interval and retain the activity fraction of the field-free reference. Calibration against the same-source field-free background h0 gives

A=hh0,Cm=h2h02,E+(x,p)≃m02A2+c02Cm2|p|2.(2.15)

Use the reference units c0=1 of this chapter. If the spatial action of light is received through the same type of package, with a common field-free speed calibration, then these two quantities admit the geometric representation [8]

ds2=A(x)2dt2−B(x)2dx2.(2.16)
E(x,p)=A(x)m02+|p|2B(x)2,|dxdt|m0=0=AB.(2.17)

Comparing the actual principal part and mass shell term by term gives the general relation and its value for this preparation:

B=ACm,Cm=A2 ⟹ B=A−1.(2.18)

The reciprocal relation follows jointly from single-package maintenance and three-package overlap. Other preparations give different outputs: the original coherent phase package and the first-order common acceptance response can give A=Cm, whereas gating maintenance without changing displacement gives Cm=1. Each configuration has its own actual action and cannot substitute for another. If the activity fraction changes, the frequency ratios also include the change in the complete cycle period.

For static nonuniform light propagation hHγ0h, the preserved transverse condition is weighted: Div(h−1ψγ)=0. Emission must enter this propagating space. A time-dependent h introduces further constraint terms. The conditional realization of Eq. (2.18) therefore does not automatically establish common geometry in a persistent time-dependent or strong background. The companion Geometric Extension and Optical Examples computes consequences of specified clock–rod and nonlinear constitutive relations; its exponential profile still requires an independent transport basis.

2.6 Nonlinear Distributions

In a weak field, background exchange can be calculated with a common reference. Near a source, background changes may also affect exchange rates and stationary weights at different positions, so transport itself varies with the field. A nonlinear field equation must incorporate this dependence into the existing flow relation.

Let ni be the transported background deficit and πi>0 the stationary weight of the same network. For exchange satisfying detailed balance, let wij be the jump rate from i to j, with conductance κij=wijπi=wjiπj. The net flow from i to j and the stationary source equation are [9]

Jij=κij(niπi−njπj),∑jJij=si.(2.19)

This form retains local occupation, stationary weight, and exchange capacity separately. Constant coefficients recover the harmonic distribution above. When the coefficients vary with the field, flow is conserved in the same way, but the spatial profile changes accordingly.

The nonlinear profile depends on how ni, πi, and κij vary jointly with the background state. Given these relations, the sources, and the boundary conditions, Eq. (2.19) determines the net flow and stationary distribution. Section S1 of the supplement gives a constitutive example yielding an exponential distribution. Dynamical Supplement D7 retains the occupation covariance and exchange coherence produced by persistent sources and transport, and bounds deviations from a time-ordered mean action. Without control of those correlations, one occupation variable does not close clock–rod and spatial propagation responses.

2.7 Time-Dependent Gravitational Fields

After a source changes, new writing enters the background cycle by cycle and propagates together with the existing distribution. A static field is the stationary result of this process under a fixed source, while the time-dependent response retains the full build-up history. For the refreshing realization of Chapter 1, write T=R(I−Dε) and qn=RDεbn. Then

ξN=TNξ0+∑n=0N−1TN−1−nqn.(2.20)

Each term represents the share of one source-writing contribution that arrives after subsequent exchanges. When the source stops writing a bias but unbiased refreshing continues, the existing bias keeps evolving under T and relaxes toward the supply state. When the source varies periodically, outputs with different delays combine to form the response. The number of propagation cycles and the total elapsed duration of each cycle jointly determine arrival and decay.

A static 1/r profile alone does not determine time-dependent behavior. For the present occupation process, R=I−cL outside the source. Converting cycles to time with the complete cycle period τ gives, in the slowly varying limit,

∂tξ=D∇2ξ,D=cℓx2τ.(2.21)

This describes transport and relaxation of the mean occupation. It can establish a harmonic static far field, while its time dependence is diffusive. The finite sequence of exchanges still specifies which positions changes reach step by step; the continuum diffusion equation describes their long-time, large-scale average [10].

Coherent propagation additionally retains amplitudes and relative phases. The original field model [11] connects gravitational radiation to directional perturbations of the common time and length scales, read through the propagation responses of light and matter. Section 5.4 and Dynamical Supplement D8 give a separate finite propagation preserving directional constraints; its material connection to the original common clocks and rods remains to be established. Equation (2.21) describes relaxation of the mean occupation.

Energy transfer in radiation remains part of the joint accounting. Changes in the source, propagating background, receiving matter, and preparation apparatus together determine the output. Where controlled actions are used, preparation and switching work must also be included.

Chapter 3. Gauge Fields and Nuclear Interactions

Electromagnetic, weak, and color interactions select exchange channels through the charges of matter. A source injects excitations and phase changes into the background, whose propagation carries them to compatible matter. Phase comparisons between positions, internal-state transfers, and momentum exchange together constitute the physical content of these fields. Interactions between nucleons likewise proceed through emission, propagation, and absorption, with internally structured composite matter at the endpoints.

3.1 Charges and Exchange

Charge specifies how matter participates in a type of interaction. For electromagnetism, take the self-adjoint operator Q in the complete matter representation as the electric-charge generator. Charge states satisfy Q|a⟩=qa|a⟩, where qa includes the elementary charge unit. Matter at both ends and the background transmitting the excitation participate jointly in exchange, and their charge changes must balance in the same process. An actual charge-preserving joint action satisfies

[Uex,QA+QB+QB]=0,qA′+qB′+qB′=qA+qB+qB.(3.1)

The second relation applies to nonzero transfer matrix elements between states of definite charge. Photons carry no electric charge: electromagnetic exchange can transfer energy and momentum while preserving the charges at both ends. Transfers involving charged modes allow the endpoint charges to change, with the exchanged component balancing the difference. Both cases are described by the same joint balance.

References [2] and [3] first establish multiplicative conservation of character charge in the joint state. The physical counterparts of electric, weak, and color charges follow Ref. [3]; this chapter uses these generators in the corresponding matter representations. Character labels specify types and transfer directions, while charge values are determined by Q. The opposite charges of antiparticles are likewise determined in the complete representation. Type conjugation, exchange direction, and charge sign thus retain their respective meanings.

Weak and color actions also change the internal states of matter. The two- and three-dimensional factors of Ref. [3] provide the structure for these matrix actions. Writing Eab=|a⟩⟨b| for a transfer within a factor gives

[Eab,Ecd]=δbcEad−δdaEcb.(3.2)

This relation explains why two successive transfers can depend on their order. Off-diagonal transfers together with relative diagonal phases provide three traceless self-adjoint directions for a two-dimensional factor and eight for a three-dimensional factor. These carry the matrix structures of weak and color interactions. Electromagnetic action is organized by the charge generator retained in the neutral action, and its actual response is read through relative phases and the motion of charged matter.

Source strength comes from the actual matrix elements and elapsed durations of these actions. An emission can change the internal source state, or leave the source unchanged after mediator retrieval while changing endpoint correlations. Reference [3] constructs resonant exchange for accessible two-level targets: with product-form carrier preparations at both ends, three joint pulses restore the mediator to its prepared state while retaining matter transfer and entanglement. Specific field vertices are constructed according to their participating carriers, charge transfer, and propagation. A persistent field connects the corresponding exchange to multiple matter systems: the source supplies channel excitations and phases, receiving matter responds through corresponding vertices, and the source undergoes back-reaction. Coupling coefficients calibrate their relative strengths, while propagation determines the spatial distribution.

3.2 Phase and Propagation

As matter passes through the background, its internal state changes segment by segment through successive exchanges. For the part of propagation that retains coherence, a transfer matrix Tji from position i to j can represent one action. Along a history γ, the segment matrices multiply in their actual order to give Tγ. In a one-dimensional internal representation, this action can be a phase; in a multidimensional representation, it can also rotate the internal state of matter.

Internal states at different positions must be expressed in their respective bases. If the components at position i are written as ψi′=Giψi, with Gi unitary, the same actual transfer is represented by

Tji′=GjTjiGi†,Tγ′=GendTγGstart†.(3.3)

Basis changes at neighboring segments cancel inside the product, leaving only transformations at its endpoints. This is the meaning of a local gauge representation in propagation: internal coordinates may be chosen at each position, and the actions connecting positions must change representation accordingly. When matter, background action, and readout are transformed together, event probabilities remain invariant.

For two coherent histories with the same start and end, their relative transfer is Tγ2†Tγ1. It transforms by conjugation at the start, so the interference term evaluated with the initial state is invariant. For a selected detection outcome, if the histories contribute amplitudes a1,a2 and leave normalized environment states |e1⟩,|e2⟩, its probability contains

p=|a1|2+|a2|2+2Re[a1a2―⟨e2|e1⟩].(3.4)

The relative phase is produced by the two actual evolutions, while visibility also depends on whether the environment distinguishes them [2,12]. When coherent retrieval restores a common environment preparation, the path phases can continue to interfere in matter. When records distinguish the histories, the cross term changes with their environment overlap. Field phase and the final record therefore belong to the same process.

Figure 3.1. Comparing propagation phases. Two histories connect the same preparation and receiver, each accumulating its actual transfer matrix; together they affect readout at the receiver. A local basis change transforms the representations of adjacent transfer matrices without changing physical probabilities. The paths depict two propagation histories of amplitudes, without implying pointwise measurements along the way. Whether the environment distinguishes them is determined by actual records.

When coherent propagation is smooth on the observation scale and local actions admit a unitary-connection description, set ℏ=c0=1 and write infinitesimal transfer as [13]

Dμ=∂μ+iAμ,Tγ=Pexp(−i∫γAμdxμ).(3.5)

Here Aμ is a self-adjoint matrix containing the coupling and charge generators, and P orders actions along propagation. The derivative Dμ compares matter components using actual transfer between neighboring positions. To preserve Eq. (3.3), the connection transforms as Aμ′=GAμG†+i(∂μG)G†. The phase connection thereby compares local representations; amplitude changes and dissipation during propagation remain calculable from the full exchange.

Comparing two orders of transfer around a small loop gives a leading difference determined by the commutator of covariant derivatives:

[Dμ,Dν]=iFμν,Fμν=∂μAν−∂νAμ+i[Aμ,Aν].(3.6)

The curvature Fμν of this propagation transforms as Fμν′=GFμνG†. In an Abelian action, the matrices commute and loop differences arise from spatial and temporal variations of the connection. Internal weak and color actions additionally retain the commutator arising from their ordering. Phase changes and internal transfers thus acquire a common field description while preserving their distinct action structures.

Connection and curvature describe the geometry of coherent transfer. Their evolution is determined by actual background action. We next construct finite flux return, complete massive transport, and color-link return, then read continuum field equations in their respective controlled windows. Mass and charge identifications are inherited from Ref. [3]. Auxiliary preparation, spatial coupling, and scale separation remain explicit conditions; standard continuum forms serve to compare the derived responses.

3.3 Electromagnetic Fields

Electromagnetic interaction connects charge transfer in matter to coherent changes in the background. As charge moves along an edge, the background carries the corresponding flux; a completed matter loop can also leave a divergence-free background change. Static storage and energy-carrying propagation must be determined together from the actual evolution of these quantities. We construct this response through finite joint exchanges; the Maxwell form follows in a controlled continuum representation.

The field equations below first use lattice units and band slow time τ; actual time and lattice spacing are restored together at the end. Fix a fundamental flux-charge unit q>0, and first consider the branch of charge q. Take Aμ=qAμ, with Aμ=(ϕ,−A) and signature (+,−,−,−). The coherent transfer phase and curvature are [14]

φγ=q∫γ(A·dx−ϕdτ),Fμν=∂μAν−∂νAμ.(3.7)

The temporal–spatial and spatial–spatial differences of the same connection give

E=−∇ϕ−∂τA,B=∇×A.(3.8)

To determine its dynamics, let D and C be the vertex–edge and edge–face incidence maps of the actual spatial graph, with DC†=0. Each edge retains a finite integer flux Ne and its truncated raising shift Ue; Wp is the ordered product of raising and lowering operators around a face. Charged matter transfer simultaneously lowers the corresponding edge flux, so the complete transfer preserves

Gx=(DN)x−ρx/q,[Gx,Hm]=0,∂τρ=−Dj.(3.9)

Here Hm includes matter maintenance and joint charged hopping, and j is the current determined by that hopping. Maintenance acts on the original matter carrier, while hopping acts jointly on matter at both ends and on the associated edge flux. All actual outputs, including failures at the flux cutoff, are retained. Equation (3.9) gives charge conservation for this complete action, preserving the subspace initially satisfying Gx=0.

Background storage follows from two actual returns. Edge flux controls a neutral two-state auxiliary; loop transport and a reference arm enter the same output of another auxiliary with opposite phase. With Yr|±⟩=±|±⟩ and σ−|+⟩=|−⟩, take

H(δ)=HR+δV+δ2Hm,HR=∑rmrYr,V=∑eλeXe⊗Ne+∑pλp[σ−,p⊗(I−Wp)+σ+,p⊗(I−Wp)†].(3.10)

The positive mr and the parameter δ specify a separation between fast maintenance and slow response. The finite exchanges of the mathematical foundation and the preparation and protection of Ref. [3] provide tools for implementing these matrix elements. Deployment on each edge and face, and preparation of the auxiliaries, are physical conditions of this construction. All auxiliaries and returns participate in the evolution. For fixed parameters, [H,Gx]=0, and the energy of the complete H is conserved.

Prepare the isolated spectral band continuously connected to the all-upper input. Leaving that input and returning through the same auxiliary gives the positive denominator 2mr; second-order cross returns through distinct auxiliaries vanish. The band action is therefore

Hband=ER+δ2H2+O(δ4),H2=Hm+12∑eaeNe2+12∑pbp(I−Wp)†(I−Wp),ae=λe2/me,bp=λp2/mp.(3.11)

The positive sign follows from this spectral preparation. The upper band has an energy and preparation cost; it is not the thermal ground state of the complete system. Choosing the lower branch changes the sign of the return shift. Section D2 of the Supplementary Dynamical Proofs gives the band isometry, remainder, and cutoff terms. Energies here refer to the corresponding actual generators; their relation to bare-shell energy requires a separate accounting of the complete implementation.

For uniform ae=a and bp=b, write Sp=(Wp−Wp†)/(2i), Kp=(Wp+Wp†)/2, and use slow time τ=δ2t. Define

Ee=aNe/q,Bp=−Sp/q,ε=q2/a,μ−1=q2b.(3.12)

Commutators with the same H2 give the finite equations

DE=ρ/ε,εE˙=μ−1C†B−j,B˙=−CE+RB,(3.13)

where

RB,p=−a2q∑eCpe{Ne,Kp−I}−iq[Hm+HB,Sp],[3pt]HB=b2∑p(I−Wp)†(I−Wp).(3.14)

Small loop phases, controlled flux fluctuations, and controlled cutoff boundaries make RB negligible relative to the leading terms. Then Wp≃ei(Cθ)p and Ae=−θe/q connect the finite readouts to Eq. (3.8). In a uniform three-dimensional long-wavelength window, this gives the Maxwell form [15]:

∇·E=ρ/ε,μ−1∇×B−ε∂τE=j,∇·B=0,∇×E+∂τB=0.(3.15)

The absence of magnetic sources follows here from cancellation of loop boundaries. At finite phases, the linear divergence of Sp need not vanish exactly. These approximations must remain valid over the time interval considered; a small initial phase alone does not guarantee this.

The same electric flux energy determines static attraction and repulsion. On a connected graph of zero total charge, let L=DD† and NL=D†L+ρ/q. Orthogonal decomposition gives

HE=12ερ†L+ρ+a2‖N−NL‖2.(3.16)

In the noncompact approximation with localized phases, flux translation preserves the loop action and shifts the entire transverse spectrum by this longitudinal energy. Finite integer flux retains sector and boundary corrections. In a three-dimensional far-field continuum window, the point-source kernel of L+ is 1/(4πr), giving

ϕ(r)=qs4πεr,V(r)=qsqt4πεr,F=qsqt4πεr2r^.(3.17)

Like charges repel and opposite charges attract through the gradient of the actual energy. The same phase in charged hopping gives Hm(A)=Hm(0)−∑eAeje(0)+O(A2). For a single-band wave packet in a slowly varying field, hold the other material parameters fixed and apply Hamilton’s equations to its actual semiclassical symbol ϵm(p−qA)+qϕ. This gives

dπdτ=q(E+v×B),π=p−qA.(3.18)

The source current and force are thus determined by one matter–background action. If the intrinsic band has additional explicit position dependence, the force also contains −(∇xϵm)π. Interband transitions, finite phases, and lattice gradients remain corrections to this semiclassical expression.

Energy exchanged between electric edges and magnetic faces cancels term by term, while work on matter has the opposite sign. In the same continuum window, the field energy flux is [16]

∂τ(ε2|E|2+12μ|B|2)+∇·(E×Bμ)=−j·E.(3.19)

Quantum readouts use symmetrized products; products of means do not replace general correlated expectations. The complete model retains auxiliary and contact energies. The quadratic field energy is the leading band expression at weak phase.

In the same fundamental charge unit, an actual edge transfer of integer charge Q=nq must carry flux action Ln,e=(Ue†)n for n≥0, or Ln,e=Ue−n for n<0, where the latter exponent is a positive integer. Thus [Ne,Ln,e]=−nLn,e. The joint jump Tn,e=hn,e⊗Ln,e preserves the same constraint DN−ρ/q, with current jn,e=iQ(Tn,e†−Tn,e). Shifts beyond a finite flux boundary vanish. Extending the charge branch requires this actual deployment.

Propagation and coupling calibration constrain the same coefficients. Let ℓ be the cubic lattice spacing and s the common conversion rate from full reference time to band time; in the autonomous Eq. (3.10), s=δ2. Transverse waves and the static energy difference in the same charge channel give

ωτ2(k)=4ab∑isin2(kiℓ/2),cfield=sℓab,αnfield=n24πa/b.(3.20)

The corresponding physical readouts are Aphys=A/ℓ, ϕphys=sϕ, Ephys=sE/ℓ, and Bphys=B/ℓ2, with source readouts ρphys=ρ/ℓ3 and jphys=sj/ℓ2. The coefficients transform together as εphys=ε/(sℓ) and μphys=μ/(sℓ). In subsequent actual-space-and-time formulas, ε,μ denote these physical coefficients. Here n is an integer in the same fundamental charge unit, and ℏ=1. Matching the light speed and corresponding coupling level of Ref. [3] requires both a product relation and a ratio relation. A common time conversion or a common matching factor on both returns leaves the dimensionless ratio unchanged. How the original matching process fixes a/b remains undetermined. The construction therefore establishes conditional electromagnetic dynamics and a calibration criterion, without treating the unresolved relative strength as a derived constant.

3.4 Weak-Interaction Fields

Weak interaction changes the internal state of matter during transmission. Denote the three traceless self-adjoint generators of the two-dimensional factor by Ta; the charges of T±=T1±iT2 are determined by the complete charge generator. Internal transfers at the source and receiver balance the charge carried by the mediator. Neutral directions retain the coherent mass construction of Ref. [3], represented in the electroweak neutral mixing basis [17,18]:

|γ⟩=sv|w⟩+cv|y⟩,|Z⟩=cv|w⟩−sv|y⟩,sv2+cv2=1.(3.21)

The two basis directions are orthonormal, with a common kinetic normalization. The relation sv2=αEM(0)/αW(0) uses the original Born-level vertex-response ratio. The common mass output couples only to the Z direction, so

Mneutral2=MZ2|Z⟩⟨Z|,Mneutral2|γ⟩=0.(3.22)

This mass identification does not by itself prescribe spatial transport. Let M be the self-adjoint bidirectional action of the original complete mass exchange, and Ξ its input–output orientation, with {M,Ξ}=0. On a three-dimensional periodic lattice, set di=Si−I. Three vector inputs are transported through one divergence and three curl auxiliaries:

Q=(d†[d]×),DQ=(0Q†Q0),Q†Q=LI3,L=∑idi†di.(3.23)

Each auxiliary retains the same mass carrier, and transport is controlled by Ξ. The actual finite action and its square are

h=M⊗I7+νΞ⊗DQ,h2=M2⊗I7+ν2I⊗DQ2.(3.24)

The three vector inputs on a mass-bright branch Mj>0 therefore share the dispersion Ωj2=Mj2+ν2L(k). All frequencies use the same actual time unit; masses already converted to complete-cycle units in Ref. [3] are not rescaled again. Spatial auxiliaries carry transport and are not counted as additional physical polarizations. Original mass-dark branches remain, with participation determined by the actual source.

Let Jj select the complete positive rest branch at the source and receiver. Equation (3.24), together with the zero input diagonal block of DQ, gives

Rj(z)=Jj†(z−h)−1Jj=z+Mjz2−Mj2−ν2LI3.(3.25)

The numerator follows from the input–output coherence retained at the actual endpoint. Coupling only the bare mass input instead gives numerator z, changing the zero-frequency response. Source, receiver, and return form one joint generator with endpoint response Σ(z)=V†(z−h)−1V. Both self returns and cross exchange must remain; the radial denominator alone is insufficient.

For Mj/ν≪1 and long-wavelength sources and receivers far from boundaries, set c=νℓ. The static denominator approaches the modified Helmholtz operator, whose continuum point-source kernel is [19]

(−c2∇2+Mj2)Gj=δ(3)(x),Gj(r)=e−Mjr/c4πc2r.(3.26)

The actual static endpoint kernel is −MjGj, combined with both endpoint strengths, orientations, and source shapes. Section D3 gives the volume normalization from lattice to continuum point sources. Mass determines the decay length c/Mj; the endpoints determine transfer type and strength. Finite lattices, transport cutoffs, and high-frequency inputs require Eq. (3.25). This construction establishes a conditional mechanism for massive propagation and short-range exchange; it does not determine weak chirality, Fermi normalization, or decay widths.

Figure 3.2. Mass and spatial interaction range. With propagation speed set to one, the figure compares the radial kernel in Eq. (3.26) and its exponential factor relative to the massless kernel. Parameters are dimensionless illustrations. The actual endpoint numerator, charge transfer, and spin response remain determined by the same joint process.

3.5 Color Fields

The order of internal color actions enters the propagation amplitude. Retain the three-dimensional color representation of Ref. [3], with self-adjoint traceless generators ta normalized by tr(tatb)=δab/2. A dynamical color connection must itself be a background object that matter can change.

Assign a finite link register to each directed edge. The operator matrix Ue transfers endpoint color, while Lea,Rea record the endpoint actions:

[La,Uij]=−tikaUkj,[Ra,Uij]=Uiktkja,[La,Rb]=0.(3.27)

Section D4 gives an explicit finite realization and its representation cutoff. Matter hopping is ψx†Ueψy+h.c., so matter and link charges jointly satisfy Gauss constraints. The nonunitarity defect of finite Ue remains in the complete action.

Form the ordered loop Wp on each actual face. Electric return couples Lea to an auxiliary carrying the corresponding adjoint charge. Magnetic return couples all nine orthogonal components of I−Wp to singlet and adjoint auxiliaries. Their color charges enter the complete Gauss generator. The same isolated upper-band return used for electromagnetism gives

H2,c=Hm,c+α2∑e,a(Lea)2+β2∑ptr[(I−Wp)†(I−Wp)],[3pt]α=λE2mE,[3pt]β=λB2mB.(3.28)

The return energy is the sum of the Gram operators of the actual outputs. Keeping the full matrix preserves noncommuting information; taking the trace of I−Wp before squaring loses the leading traceless curvature. The complete action conserves total color charge and energy. Electric flux and loop energies can exchange even without an externally prescribed source.

In a smooth, nearly unitary window with controlled cutoff, write Ui≃eiℓAi. Expansion in the specified path order gives

Wij=I+iℓ2Fij+O(ℓ3),Fij=∂iAj−∂jAi+i[Ai,Aj].(3.29)

Substitution in Eq. (3.28) gives leading magnetic Gram term ℓ4trFij2. With continuum conjugate variable Πia=−Lea/ℓ2, counting each unoriented face once gives κE=αℓ and κB=βℓ/2. The same band action yields

∂τAi=κEΠi,[3pt]∂τΠi=κBDjFji−ji,[3pt]DiΠi=ρ,[3pt]DiX=∂iX+i[Ai,X].(3.30)

This is the Yang–Mills principal part of the constructed response [20]. Source current comes from the same matter hopping, and covariant charge balance is compatible with the field equations. The commutator expresses the field's own participation in color transfer. The finite model uses complete ordered loops and actual commutators; continuum notation does not remove its cutoff corrections.

Color singlets, gluon directions, and confinement in the specified separation process remain inherited from Ref. [3]. This section supplies finite color-field dynamics and its continuum working window. It does not identify the minimal finite encoding with a continuum limit or add claims of universal confinement, a nonperturbative mass gap, or coupling running.

3.6 Nuclear Interactions

Nuclear interaction connects two complete nucleons. The pion mass determines the propagation scale, whereas nucleon spin, isospin, and spatial coupling determine direction and attraction or repulsion. Both endpoints remain present throughout, and the nucleons and pion jointly carry the charge changes in emission and absorption.

Let JN embed the nucleon carrier of Ref. [3], comprising the collective mode, color singlet, and four-state isospin–spin representation. On its three constituent slots, define Si=∑jσji and Ta=∑jτja. The complete nucleon satisfies

SiTaJN=JN(τa⊗σi).(3.31)

This collective action preserves the four nucleon states and differs from a sum of spin–isospin products on individual slots. The pion retains its original color singlet, pseudoscalar 0− identification, and isospin triplet. Equal, oppositely phased spatial arms preserve parity and enter the same complete output, giving the actual momentum vertex

Va(k)=gπτaσ·k^,k^i=sin(kiℓ)/ℓ.(3.32)

Spin and isospin arise from the complete nucleon action, while the odd momentum factor comes from cancellation between neighboring arms. The coefficient gπ is the actual exchange strength. Equal strengths on three axes and isospin covariance are deployment conditions, not consequences of charge conservation alone.

The pion uses its original complete mass exchange with one scalar spatial input and three gradient transport auxiliaries. Its complete positive rest input has propagation matrix element

Rπ(z)=z+mπz2−mπ2−ν2L,Rπ(0)=−mπ(mπ2+ν2L)−1.(3.33)

Two nucleons and a zero/one-pion capacity form the declared finite system. With V=VA+VB, its joint generator and complete return are

Hjoint=(HNNV†VHQ),Σ(z)=V†(z−HQ)−1V.(3.34)

The block HQ retains both nucleons and the pion's mass, position, and transport auxiliaries. Self returns and cross returns coexist. Exchange paths not distinguished by the complete record add as amplitudes. Joint charge and total energy are conserved by the same action. The specified capacity, shared output, and low-energy regime with weak endpoint coupling delimit the construction.

For static response, equal masses within the pion triplet, and a uniform inversion-symmetric background, take the same real strength gπ at both endpoints and set G=(mπ2+ν2L)−1 and Di=(Si−Si†)/(2iℓ). The cross response is

VAB=−2gπ2mπ(τA·τB)∑ijσAiσBj⟨DiδxA,GDjδxB⟩.(3.35)

The factor two comes from the two directions of cross return. Equation (3.34) also gives both self energies; their presence does not imply attraction in every channel. Static elimination requires external frequencies and endpoint strengths below the accessible mediator gap, with nucleon motion slow relative to the mediator response.

For mπ/ν≪1, in a long-wavelength window away from lattice and boundary scales, let c=νℓ, κ=mπ/c, and Y=e−κr/(4πc2r). The continuum point-source strength is gc=gπℓ3/2. For r>0, Eq. (3.35) becomes

VAB(r)=2gc2mπ3(τA·τB)Y(r)×[κ2σA·σB+(κ2+3κr+3r2)S12],S12=3(σA·r^)(σB·r^)−σA·σB.(3.36)

The central and tensor terms follow jointly from the same endpoints and propagation and can be compared with the corresponding meson-exchange structures [21,22]. The central term attracts for total isospin and spin (I,S)=(1,0),(0,1), and repels for (0,0),(1,1). The triplet tensor term further distinguishes directions and orbital components. Identical nucleons require fermionic antisymmetry. At the origin one must retain the finite kernel or the contact term of the same distribution, rather than extend the far-field expression to zero separation.

Section D5 supplies the complete nucleon intertwiner, finite kernel, contact term, and error bound. The result explains channel-dependent interaction in a nucleon–pion joint process. It does not yet include multipion nuclear forces, all short-range interactions, or nuclear bound-state spectra.

Chapter 4. Fields and Light

Light connects interactions to distant measurements. Emitting matter transfers energy and phase into propagating optical modes, from which receiving matter acquires a response; during propagation, changes in the background alter the phase, direction, and arrival time of light. Light therefore participates in both field propagation and field observation. Its zero rest mass, electrical neutrality, and role as a measurement signal arise, respectively, from the adopted modes, couplings, and recording processes.

4.1 Light Propagation and Phase

Chapter 3 inherits the original photon zero mode from the neutral mass response and derives two transverse propagation components in the controlled continuum window of flux and loop return. Plane waves occur in a source-free uniform region. With ℏ=c0=1, this continuum description gives

a(x,t)=ϵei(k·x−ωt),k·ϵ=0,ω=cfield|k|.(4.1)

A localized wave packet is a superposition of these components. Phase differences between neighboring wave numbers determine how the envelope moves, with group velocity vg=∇kω. The photon energy and momentum are calibrated in the same physical units as Eγ=ω and pγ=k. Zero rest mass allows all of the energy to take the form of propagation energy; it does not eliminate either the energy or its action on receiving matter.

Equation (4.1) uses the declared continuum working window of Chapter 3. Reference units c0=1 do not automatically set cfield to one; cfield=c0 remains a matching condition with the original physical calibration. The phase of the actual discrete propagation is still given by the complete cycle, and the group velocity is calculated using the total elapsed duration; at finite wave number, the actual dispersion of the adopted shift action must be retained [2,3]. The long-wavelength speed and frequency of light are calibrated together by this propagation.

The phases of matter and light can be compared using their respective continuum dispersions. Let cs denote the actual speed coefficient of the branch under consideration. On the positive-energy branch E=cs2|p|2+m2, vg=cs2p/E. Along the trajectory of the wave-packet center, the rate of change of the plane-wave phase S=p·x−Et is

E=p·vg+m2E,dSdt=−m2E.(4.2)

The right-hand side gives the residual phase accumulation along this trajectory. Let τp be proper time in the continuum clock representation of this massive branch. At rest, this rate of change is −m; for moving massive matter, it equals −mdτp/dt. Light satisfies m=0, so this phase-change rate vanishes along a light ray, and the same wavefront extends with propagation. A detector at a fixed position still encounters successive wavefronts at frequency ω and can therefore measure the frequency of light. The phase change along a light ray is thus distinguished from the frequency reading of a fixed apparatus.

Contact between light and matter occurs at the emission and reception vertices. The motion of charged matter can excite electromagnetic modes, which in turn change the state and momentum of local matter upon reaching the receiver. Energy transfer in a complete process also includes recoil, changes in internal energy levels, and supply from the apparatus. Free propagation and the exchanges at both ends are connected within the same joint evolution, from whose final state the actual pointer reads out an outcome.

4.2 Light Generation, Source Writing, and Response

Zero photon charge does not prevent charged matter from exciting the light field. Matter moving along an actual edge changes background flux. A loop return can restore matter position while leaving a divergence-free background excitation. A three-dimensional local curl deployment places the earliest output and the single-pattern response with returns in transverse propagation; the complete multiple-pattern action remains in the same model. Matter current, background generation, and reverse absorption all arise from one joint action.

One finite realization carries the source on two tree edges and closes the loop with a third. Write the tree source as Htree, the closing edge as V, and contact plus distant transport as HB. After preparing a releasable coherent combination in the original source spectrum, the complete action obeys

H=Htree+V+HB,ddt⟨Htree+V+HB⟩=0.(4.3)

The source spectrum and lowering matrix element follow from the original mass and edge strength. Work for phase preparation and restoration of control must be included. Amplitudes generated at different times combine within the same propagation. With H0=Htree+HB,

|Ψ(t)⟩=e−itH0|Ψ0⟩−i∫0te−i(t−s)H0V|Ψ(s)⟩ds.(4.4)

This gives finite-time matching between source-lowering and propagation frequencies while retaining returns and source depletion. Section D1 supplies the loop matrices, actual source preparation, and positive earliest distant net energy output. That output includes the positive and negative frequencies and multiple patterns allowed by the original action. It is not thereby a pure single photon, and conservation of the activity generator does not replace the separate bare-shell energy accounting. The background-maintenance construction of Chapter 3 additionally gives electromagnetic storage and continuum response; the extra deployments of the two constructions are stated separately.

The gravitational background written by light or moving matter is determined by contact between the source and a fresh auxiliary. Let Ks be the source generator actually coupled to it, with input ρs. For a matter source, the contact uses the maintenance and motion part on the complete carrier; function readout in the matter representation follows from the intertwining relation in Chapter 1. The read–exchange process of that chapter gives

bs=12Tr[ρssin(2treadKs)],Δξs=εs(bs−ξs).(4.5)

For a small read angle, bs=tread⟨Ks⟩+O(tread3‖Ks‖3). On a spectral branch with source-generator eigenvalue ϵs>0, the finite-angle output is 12sin(2treadϵs), proportional to ϵs in the linear readout regime; its complete-cycle energy uses the timing convention in Chapter 1. Motion can therefore produce nonzero writing for massless matter. Meanwhile, the specified common clock–rod preparation of Chapter 2 has long-wavelength reception energy E(A,p)=m2A2+A4|p|2. Its conjugate response to availability at the field-free baseline satisfies

∂E(A,p)∂A|A=1=m2+2|p|2E=E+p·v.(4.6)

The writing in Eq. (4.5) and the reception contribution in Eq. (4.6) concern different observables. Persistent evolution also retains contributions from the background's own action. The conjugate response cannot be substituted for net occupation injection.

To retain source, transport, and target reception simultaneously, use the finite joint action

Htot=Ks+Href+HB+Vw+Htr+HC,[3pt]ddt⟨Ks+Href+HB+Vw+Htr+HC⟩=0.(4.7)

Here Href retains the original background-reference action still participating during this interval, HB is the energy of the newly introduced background network, Htr transports its resource packages, and HC acts on receiving matter. The original matter background reference and this network remain distinct. If the readout contact also includes the reference action, that contribution enters Eq. (4.5) as well. Changes in every term follow from the same commutator, with source–background correlations retained. Section D7 gives the time-ordered mean-response bound in an evolving environment and the occupation covariance and exchange coherence in the three-package coefficient.

A three-dimensional local light source must also respect the propagation constraint. If Kγ is the original transverse propagation and Px a position projector, the direct action {Px,Kγ}/2 generally fails to preserve bare transversality. For a fixed positive energy scale Λ>0 independent of the input energy, the two-sided curl action KγPxKγ/Λ preserves it but sums to Kγ2/Λ, changing the source spectrum to E2/Λ. Thus the finite mechanism for a complete moving source is established, while arbitrary three-dimensional local light writing, control of persistent correlations, and a universal strong-field constitutive relation still require a common realization.

4.3 Free Radiation and Composite Sources

Freely propagating radiation and radiation confined within matter participate in different complete processes. The components of a free stream propagate individually; when radiation is confined within a composite system, it repeatedly exchanges momentum and energy with the boundary or internal matter, and the matter maintaining the confinement also participates in the overall response. The object treated as the source must be consistent with this complete process.

Using the local continuum dispersion of Section 4.1, describe a free particle stream by a distribution function f(x,p) and calculate momentum flux with the actual group velocity vg=∇pE. Let dΓp be the momentum measure with the same normalization convention. The energy density and spatial stress are

ρE=∫dΓpfE,Πij=∫dΓpfpivgj.(4.8)

For the linear light dispersion Eγ=cfield|p|, one has p·vg=Eγ, so free light satisfies trΠ=ρE: it transfers momentum as well as energy. When radiation is confined by a boundary or by internal matter, its stress must be accounted for together with the action of the confining matter.

The rest mass of composite matter is read from its total energy. If the complete state at rest satisfies HC|ΨC⟩=M|ΨC⟩, then HC includes both the interaction energy and the matter providing the constraints. Under the source calibration of the total generator in Chapter 2, it is M that enters the source relation at rest. For example, after a closed container absorbs and retains radiation, its mass change, evaluated in the same rest reference frame, equals the net retained energy; the energy balances of the emitting apparatus and the surroundings are accounted for separately. The zero rest mass of the internal photons does not eliminate the increase in total energy.

In a flat continuum representation that neglects self-gravity, if the complete system has a stress–energy tensor satisfying ∂μTμν=0, stationarity in the rest frame provides a useful balance relation. For a localized system at rest, with no external support and a time-independent stress–energy tensor, ∂kTkj=0, and the surface term at infinity vanishes. Integrating ∂k(xiTkj) gives

∫d3xTij=0,∫d3xT00=M.(4.9)

This integral relation is Laue's theorem for a system at rest [23]. The total stress includes internal radiation, interactions, and confining matter. The pressure of the internal light is balanced together with the stresses of the container or binding structure, while the total rest mass is determined by the complete energy.

The propagation energy of free radiation, the rest mass of a composite system, and the actual source writing thus each refer to a definite object. Which matter and exchanges are included in a system, and which boundaries provide its constraints, determine how its source should be accounted for.

4.4 Light, Clocks, and Length Scales

As light propagates through the background, it connects the calibrations of time and length at different positions. When light and matter share the static isotropic geometry of Section 2.5, ds2=A2dt2−B2dx2. In the geometric-optics regime [24], write the phase as S, with kμ=∂μS denoting its gradient. Massless propagation satisfies

gμνkμkν=0,E∞=−∂tS,ωloc=E∞A,|k|loc=|∇S|B.(4.10)

Here E∞ is the frequency relative to the distant reference time; in a static background, it is conserved along propagation without additional frequency conversion. A local apparatus at rest reads out ωloc using its own time and the wave number using its local length scale, with ωloc=|k|loc. The local speed of light is therefore one, whereas its coordinate speed is A/B. The two readings use different scales.

This makes the redshift relation of Chapter 2 a direct signal comparison. The local frequencies at emission and reception are E∞/Ae and E∞/Ar, respectively, so ωr/ωe=Ae/Ar. When a signal travels from a region of lower clock rate to one of higher clock rate, the receiver reads a lower frequency. Successive wavefronts maintain the same coordinate-time interval, while the clocks at the two ends assign different local durations to that interval.

Figure 4.1. Light signals connect clock comparisons. In a static background, two emissions are separated by the same reference duration Δt, and the corresponding receptions are also separated by Δt. The local clocks at the two ends record AeΔt and ArΔt, respectively, yielding the frequency ratio Ae/Ar.
