The slanted lines indicate only the signal connection from earlier emission to later reception; their slopes do not specify the coordinate speed along the path.

The arrival time of light also reads out the spatial length scale. The null-interval condition gives

dt=nopt(x)dℓ,nopt=BA,Tγ=∫γnoptdℓ.(4.11)

Here dℓ=|dx|, and Tγ is the reference propagation time along the path. The optical refractive index nopt is given by the relation between the time and length scales. Light paths vary according to this optical length, and a difference in propagation time between two paths can be converted into a phase difference. Round-trip signals connect emission, reflection, and reception into a distance measurement; gravitational time delay can be tested through such round-trip timing [25].

For static propagation between the same fixed endpoints, a small change in the optical refractive index produces the following leading change in propagation time along the zeroth-order stationary light path γ:

δT=∫γδnoptdℓ,δφ=E∞δT.(4.12)

Stationarity with fixed endpoints ensures that the path variation contributes no additional first-order optical-path term. The second equation compares monochromatic propagation phases at fixed distant frequency E∞ and a common detection time; a comparison of wave-packet arrival times reads out the first equation directly. Propagation time and deflection therefore both read out spatial changes in B/A, with their specific magnitudes determined by the actual propagation action.

Local rod length, remote round-trip distance, and coordinate separation are each determined by their corresponding operations. In a sufficiently small neighborhood, round-trip timing calibrates length using the local speed of light; across a region with a changing clock rate, the path integral in Eq. (4.11) must be retained. The emitting and receiving apparatuses, the phase of light, and the background remain within the same joint state. Observational spacetime organizes these internal processes into comparable distances and times.

4.5 Optical Recording

Upon reaching the receiver, light changes the apparatus through an actual coupling. Energy absorption, scattering, polarization selection, and phase comparison can correspond to different recording schemes; which distinctions the apparatus retains is determined by its pointer and the subsequent process that preserves the record. The record construction in Ref. [2] allows general auxiliary degrees of freedom to serve as these pointers. Light is an important carrier of signals and energy between separated positions, while a specific record is formed jointly by the light and the apparatus.

For a normalized optical input state ργ, let Mr†Mr denote the outcome effect determined by the fixed apparatus preparation and contact process. Including the no-detection outcome, the outcomes satisfy [5]

pr=Tr(ργMr†Mr),∑rMr†Mr=I.(4.13)

The detection probability therefore includes the matching between the incident mode and the apparatus, the coupling duration, the acceptance range, and the detection efficiency [26]. The electromagnetic coupling enters the contact amplitude; its numerical value is not itself the probability of producing a record in each cycle. Changes in the energy and momentum of the receiver are also read from the same output.

Phase is recorded through comparison. Consider an ideal interferometer with equal-weight beam splitting and recombination, balanced losses in the two arms, and identical detection efficiencies at the two outputs. Let the two histories accumulate a phase difference Δφ at the receiver, and include the phase of the environment overlap in θenv. The conditional probabilities of the two complementary outputs are then

p±=12[1±Vcos(Δφ+θenv)],V=|⟨e2|e1⟩|≤1.(4.14)

Here the probabilities have been normalized to the light that successfully arrives; actual losses remain included in Eq. (4.13). The field changes the phase along the paths, and the interferometer converts this change into a change in the probabilities of the two outcomes. When the environment retains a distinction between the paths, V decreases, changing the extent to which the phase information can be read out. The detected event and the preceding coherent propagation are connected within the same process.

Repeated records form statistical readings of the field. Let Xa denote a counting outcome in trial a, and let N=∑aXa. Then

VarN=∑aVarXa+2∑a<bCov(Xa,Xb).(4.15)

Correlations in the source and apparatus enter the second term. Independent, identically distributed counts give the usual square-root fluctuation scaling; when correlations are present, the actual covariances must be used. The intensity, phase, and polarization of light can thus be reconstructed through various statistics [26,27]; readings of a continuous field are formed from actual events and their correlations.

Chapter 5. Field Phenomena

The spatial distribution of a field manifests itself through matter motion, energy exchange, and instrument records. The action on distant matter must pass through background propagation; the response produced by light at the receiver must pass through the actual coupling between light and the apparatus; and continuously varying field quantities are read out through the apparatus's comparisons and statistics of these processes.

5.1 Long-Range Action

A persistent source can maintain a measurable action at a distant position. Immediately after the source changes, however, the distant region does not acquire the new stationary value. The stationary distribution describes the spatial relation after the persistent action has been established, while the build-up process retains the time required for each segment of propagation.

The background recurrence of Chapter 2 directly connects these two aspects. Fix the refreshing and transport rules, and let T=R(I−Dε), qn=RDεbn. Comparing two source histories with the same initial state gives

δξN=∑n=0N−1TN−1−nδqn.(5.1)

Each source change first forms δqn in the current cycle and then undergoes propagation over the remaining cycles. For an implementation that transports by at most one neighboring position per cycle, Tij=0 whenever positions i,j are neither identical nor adjacent. Denoting the shortest number of steps on this actual exchange graph by d(i,j), we have

(Tk)ij=0when d(i,j)>k.(5.2)

This follows directly from a finite number of local exchanges: before the required number of steps has elapsed, no sequence of actions has yet carried the change at that position to the receiver. The starting point in Eq. (5.1) is the support of the current-cycle output qn, which already includes the transport step performed after source writing. The number of steps here is converted into elapsed duration using the actual exchanges and complete timing.

If the boundary supply makes propagation in this finite system decay, the long-term action of a constant source gives

ξ*=(I−T)−1q=∑k=0∞Tkq.(5.3)

The long-range stationary response accumulates over many cycles of propagation. The three-dimensional far-field 1/r kernel of Chapter 2 is precisely the long-term distribution obtained in the corresponding spatial structure; it does not remove the temporal ordering in the finite-duration solution.

Figure 5.1. A distant response undergoes successive local propagation. The left panel starts with a unit perturbation at the center of a one-dimensional chain. In each cycle, it remains at the same position with weight 1/2 and is transported to either side with weight 1/4. The area of each dot represents the response weight, and the dashed lines mark the range reached by traversing at most one neighboring position per cycle. The right panel reads out a unit four steps away: there is no response before step 4, after which different propagation histories accumulate a nonzero weight. This is a finite-step example of Eq. (5.2).

A coherent field propagates according to its own evolution equation. For the linear electromagnetic field of Chapter 3, in Lorenz gauge and with boundary conditions excluding any additional incident field, the retarded solution for a conserved current is

ϕ(t,x)=∫d3x′ρ(t−R/c,x′)4πεR,A(t,x)=μ∫d3x′j(t−R/c,x′)4πR,R=|x−x′|.(5.4)

Here the fields and coefficients are physical quantities measured in actual reference time, with c=cfield=1/εμ. Each contribution reaching the receiver at time t is evaluated at the corresponding retarded source time. Once the source and current cease to change, this reduces to the static kernel. The diffusion description of occupation and this coherent-wave description represent different responses; similarity in their static forms does not by itself determine their dispersion or propagation speeds. The temporal structure of long-range action is always given by the actual propagation.

5.2 The Photoelectric Effect

When light illuminates matter, the incident energy can become internal excitation, heat, or scattered light, and it can also cause electrons to escape from the surface. The photoelectric effect corresponds to the electron-emission channel: the material absorbs light, an electron overcomes the energy difference required to escape its binding, and the collection apparatus produces a current or an individual count.

The energy transferred in a single event is determined by the joint action. The energy-conserving exchange in Ref. [2] gives an explicit expression. If the incoming and outgoing auxiliary states have energies εi,εo, and the corresponding matter transition operator is Joi, then

[HS,Joi]=(εi−εo)Joi.(5.5)

Here HS is the matter energy in the chosen conserving exchange, and the corresponding matter transition receives the energy lost by the auxiliary. Shell-energy exchange uses the shell generator to determine transition energy differences; absorption using the complete maintenance and motion action is checked against the corresponding joint contact. The optical-absorption energy balance uses the actual photon energy ℏω and the material escape threshold, with the material, electron, and recoil jointly receiving the change. This section retains ℏ explicitly.

In the weak-light regime dominated by single-photon absorption, define the material's work function W by the lowest-energy escape channel. Then

ℏω=W+Ke+Eextra,Eextra≥0,Kmax≃ℏω−W.(5.6)

Here Eextra includes additional excitation, recoil, and losses relative to the lowest-energy channel. The last relation takes the upper edge of the kinetic energy where these additional costs are negligible, recovering Einstein's photoelectric relation [28]. When the single-photon energy is below W, this escape channel is closed, although the material may still absorb or scatter light through other channels. Above threshold, the frequency determines how much energy a single absorption can provide.

The light intensity I is the energy arriving per unit time and unit area. For incident light of fixed frequency illuminating an area S uniformly for a duration T, let η be the efficiency with which an incident photon produces one collected primary photoelectron. In the single-photon regime, with the material state and efficiency maintained and the apparatus not yet saturated,

⟨Ne⟩=ηISTℏω.(5.7)

Increasing the light intensity therefore primarily increases the number of collected electrons, whereas changing the frequency changes the energy available in a single event and determines whether the material's emission threshold is crossed. The efficiency η is given by the actual absorption, electron transport, and collection processes and may also depend on frequency; it connects to the detection apparatus of Chapter 4.

Figure 5.2. Frequency and light intensity affect different outputs. The left panel shows the ideal upper edge of the kinetic energy in Eq. (5.6): this single-photon escape channel is absent in the region ℏω/W<1. The right panel shows how the count in Eq. (5.7) varies with light intensity at fixed frequency and efficiency. The curves are normalized by an arbitrary positive reference intensity I0 and its count N0, without introducing specific material parameters; multiphoton processes and saturation lie outside the scope of these two relations.

The apparatus can reduce its output to “detected” and “not detected,” or it can further resolve the electron's energy and direction. A binary outcome can combine many different energy transfers. The energy transferred is determined by the actual transition, while the binary character specifies only which distinction the apparatus retains. The amplitudes of continuous propagation determine the probabilities of the channels, while individual absorption and subsequent recording produce countable events.

5.3 Energy Transfer by Fields

A source loses energy when it emits radiation, receiving matter gains energy when it absorbs radiation, and the intervening propagation belongs to the same process. The common background, propagating excitations, interactions, and auxiliaries involved in preparation and retrieval all enter the complete Hamiltonian. Denoting this Hamiltonian by Htot(t), we have

ddt⟨Htot⟩=⟨∂Htot∂t⟩.(5.8)

For a complete closed system with no external time-dependent control, the right-hand side vanishes. If prescribed switching or driving is used, the right-hand side is the corresponding control power; once the driving apparatus is included in a larger closed system, this exchange also becomes part of joint energy conservation. The supply required for source maintenance and background refreshing therefore cannot be omitted from the energy balance.

Local energy flux describes how energy crosses the boundary of a region. The electromagnetic model of Chapter 3 gives uem=ε|E|2/2+|B|2/(2μ) and Sem=E×B/μ. All quantities here use physical readouts and coefficients in actual time. Integrating over a fixed region V yields

ddt∫Vuemd3x=−∮∂VSem·da−∫Vj·Ed3x.(5.9)

Field energy within the region can increase through inflow across the boundary and decrease through outflow or work done on matter. The energy acquired by the receiving material and apparatus is connected to the field through the final term. Even when no detector is placed along the propagation path, the field state and these energy flows are still given by the evolution; recording determines which quantities the apparatus retains, not whether the propagating energy exists.

For other fields, local energy and energy flux must be determined from the corresponding actions. The finite net energy of directional radiation is calculated in Supplement D8; persistent far-field power and positive-definite macroscopic energy still require the same propagation and actual material identification. Conservation for the full system specifies the total balance, while the specific distribution is determined by the propagation dynamics.

5.4 Directional Radiation and Interferometric Observation

The directional action of matter can change background shear response. Free radiation additionally requires an actual propagation carrier, a source action, and constraints preserved by both. We consider an explicit conditional construction, distinguishing absorption of radiation from its connection to a geometric change in the original material clocks and rods.

A symmetric tensor amplitude T∈Sym2(C3) carries six directional components, alongside a separate unexcited state and two propagation arms. It differs from the density readout of a single direction package. For centered-difference symbol di=sin(kiℓ)/ℓ, set C=i[d]× and LT=(CT+TCT)/2. Take the local propagation and source operator

hg=icg(0L−L0),B3(J)=L(CJCT).(5.10)

The three-difference combination satisfies DivB3=0 and trB3=0. Coupling it to the actual energy-lowering block of matter, while retaining adjoint return and a receiver of the same type, makes source, propagation, and absorption jointly preserve the transverse traceless constraints. For |d|≠0, the constrained positive-frequency space has dimension two. Other free modes and negative-frequency branches remain in the complete background. Preparing this invariant sector does not mean evolution attracts arbitrary inputs into it.

The same finite action can produce positive short-time net field energy, excite a receiver, and distinguish polarization. Each actual port carries a |d|3 filter, which cannot be divided out at emission or reception. Section D8 gives the full free spectrum, two-end response, and energy balance. Persistent far-field power, positive-definite macroscopic radiation energy, and a common calibration of cg with light speed have not yet been established.

The material connection imposes an additional requirement. The natural two-index lift of the original directional readout gives q~(T)=Re(TT†)−‖T‖2I/3. At fixed propagation direction n=d/|d|, every transverse traceless amplitude satisfies

q~(T)=‖T‖2(I6−nnT2).(5.11)

This reads only intensity in that direction and cannot distinguish equally intense linear polarizations. The actual original material contact also generates trace or longitudinal components. A coherent reference can provide a first-order readout under a specified preparation, but its formation and constraint-preserving service have not been completed. The radiation candidate therefore cannot directly be identified with a first-order geometric perturbation of the original clocks and rods.

Interferometry describes the subsequent readout: once complete matter and light propagation determine the optical-path changes of both arms, the returning phase difference becomes a detector output [29]. This relation can be stated independently, but does not replace the dynamical connection from directional radiation to actual optical paths.

To illustrate this relation, consider an ideal Michelson interferometer with two equal-length arms, each completing one round trip. In the regime where the perturbation varies slowly compared with the round-trip time, let δL1,δL2 denote the equivalent changes in the one-way optical lengths of the two arms, and set ΔL=δL1−δL2. Calibrating the laser wavelength λ and ΔL with the same reference time and length scales, and keeping the laser frequency fixed, gives

δφ=2kΔL=4πλΔL,k=2πλ.(5.12)

The round trip in each arm doubles the optical-path change relative to a one-way passage. Here ΔL is obtained from the complete light paths and the response of the test bodies. For faster variations, the actual round-trip histories must be integrated, retaining time delays and the frequency response of the instrument. The static optical-path relation of Chapter 4 is the static case of this description.

At the point of maximum slope of the interference output in Eq. (4.14), fix the visibility at V>0 and estimate a small phase change from N independent, successfully detected outcomes. At this point, p+=1/2, the standard deviation of its count fraction is 1/(2N), and the magnitude of the phase slope is V/2. Thus

σφ≃1VN,σΔL≃λ4πVN.(5.13)

This gives the counting-noise term for an ideal single-round-trip apparatus [30]. Multiple round trips, optical cavities, noise in the source and apparatus, and correlated states of light change the actual response and uncertainty. A smaller perturbation produces a smaller change in the output probabilities; accumulating many records allows this change to be distinguished from statistical fluctuations.

The continuous motion of interference fringes describes a change in a statistical distribution, while photon counting describes the absorption processes used to read it out. These two readings belong to different stages of the same measurement chain.

5.5 Formation of Classical Fields

Macroscopic field readings are stable because the apparatus produces a reproducible response over a certain spatial and temporal range and estimates its mean quantities through many records. A continuum representation of the field further requires sufficiently smooth spatial variation within that range. Statistical stability and spatial smoothness together allow an instrument of finite resolution to describe the field by a continuous function.

Consider the statistics first. Let Xa be a real-valued reading in a sequence of records, with a common mean, variance σ2>0, and lag correlation coefficients ρk under a stationary preparation. Averaging M records, Eq. (4.15) can be rearranged as

VarX¯M=σ2M[1+2∑k=1M−1(1−kM)ρk].(5.14)

Independent records make the bracket equal to one, and the uncertainty of the mean decreases as M−1/2. The same leading scaling holds when the correlation tail is summable and the asymptotic variance coefficient is nonzero; if the source or matter retains long-term memory, the correlation terms must be estimated together. Replacing the auxiliary with a fresh one in every cycle specifies only the preparation of the fresh auxiliary; it does not erase correlations retained in the matter and the existing background.

Now consider space. A continuum equation approximates a specific discrete propagation. For example, for a uniform one-dimensional centered difference with spacing ℓ, a sufficiently smooth field quantity f satisfies

f(x+ℓ)−2f(x)+f(x−ℓ)ℓ2=f″(x)+ℓ212f(4)(x)+O(ℓ4).(5.15)

When the scale of field variation is much larger than ℓ, the leading differential term describes spatial variation on larger scales, and higher derivatives provide corrections. Source points, boundaries, and sharply varying interfaces still require the corresponding local solutions. This expansion is determined by the discrete operator and the smoothness of the field; its scale cannot be assigned solely from a cycle frequency.

After a mean has been read out stably, the equation it obeys is still determined by the dynamics. The refreshing recurrence with fixed coefficients in Chapter 2 and the linear Maxwell principal part obtained in the controlled window of Chapter 3 allow averaging to commute with the linear action, so the corresponding mean quantities evolve under the same linear equations. Nonlinear actions retain contributions from fluctuations. For example, for two classical statistical field quantities F,G,

⟨FG⟩=⟨F⟩⟨G⟩+⟨δFδG⟩.(5.16)

Increasing the number of observations allows the terms on the right-hand side to be estimated more accurately, but does not automatically eliminate the correlation term. In the regime where fluctuations are small relative to a slowly varying background and correlation terms can be controlled, the mean field can approximately form a closed classical description; if correlations still play a significant role, the corresponding correlation quantities must also be retained.

The continuum equations of classical fields are determined by these averaging processes, and their accuracy depends on statistical fluctuations, spatial variation scales, and the degree of mean-field closure.

Chapter 6. Source Response and Tests

Source writing determines the local input, while propagation and return determine how this input accumulates and builds up. Comparing finite readout, stationary distributions, and temporal responses allows contact and transport to be examined separately and tests whether they belong to the same process.

6.1 Finite Source Readout

Consider the fixed eigenstate source of Chapter 2, keeping the readout procedure, update probability, and supply boundary unchanged. Let χ=2treadλs. Equations (1.2) and (2.4) give bs=sinχ/2 and the actual net source js. Define the linear reference by the zero-phase slope of the same process, js,lin=χ(∂js/∂χ)χ=0. Then

jsjs,lin=sinχχ=1−χ26+O(χ4).(6.1)

This ratio also applies to the far-field amplitude at the same position. The return kernel and refreshing coefficient remain in both outputs and cancel in the ratio; if the supply boundary or update probability changes, their effect on the absolute amplitude is still given by Eq. (2.4). The sinusoidal relation is the full output of this bounded readout and is not monotonic over the full phase range. This relation tests the finite-readout correction for this source contact. The output for a general source spectral distribution is obtained from Eq. (4.5).

6.2 Build-up and Periodic Response

The temporal response uses the same propagation matrix T. Suppose a constant source changes at some instant and thereafter maintains the new q. The deviation from the new stationary state is

ξN−ξ*=TN(ξ0−ξ*).(6.2)

This equation describes both build-up and restoration. If a resolvable mode has a propagation eigenvalue 0<ζ<1 and each complete cycle has elapsed duration τ, it decays as ζN, corresponding to a relaxation time −τ/logζ. The static accumulation factor of the same mode under persistent input is 1/(1−ζ). Greater accumulation and slower restoration are thus linked through the same eigenvalue.

Periodic modulation allows both amplitude and delay to be read out. For ξn+1=Tξn+qn, take qn=Re(qωe−iωnτ). The stable periodic response ξn=Re(Xωe−iωnτ) satisfies

Xω=(e−iωτI−T)−1qω.(6.3)

At zero frequency, this reduces to the stationary response (I−T)−1; as the frequency increases, the response amplitude and phase begin to resolve the temporal structure of propagation. For the single mode above, denote the ratio of the complex response amplitude to the complex source-input amplitude by Hζ(ω). Then

Hζ(ω)=1e−iωτ−ζ,|Hζ(ω)Hζ(0)|=1−ζ(1−ζ)2+4ζsin2(ωτ/2).(6.4)

A stationary measurement obtains only the zero-frequency response; an additional measurement of the build-up curve or periodic phase can test the propagation process that produces this distribution. An actual probe generally reads out multiple modes simultaneously, with weights determined by the source position, input procedure, and receiving coupling. What is tested here is the relaxation and accumulation of occupation transport.

A test can first determine the linear slope through small-phase readout and then compare the output at finite phase. Alternatively, one set of time-domain or frequency-domain responses can determine the propagation parameters, which are then used to calculate another set of responses. The readout phase and the total elapsed duration of each cycle require independent calibration, while the source and probe couplings remain consistent. In this way, the constraints imposed by the same propagation operator across different observations become relations that can be checked.

Chapter 7. Conclusions

A field is the distribution of background states and correlations formed through the joint exchange of matter and background. Source matter changes the background, local propagation carries this change to other positions, and receiving matter acquires changes in phase, energy, and momentum through its own coupling. After formation, matter retains the accompanying resources required for maintenance and motion; source and reception actions are connected through this complete carrier. The source output, field propagation, and action on matter thus belong to the same physical process; back-reaction, return, and energy exchange on all sides remain in the complete joint evolution.

Static and time-dependent fields are two manifestations of this process. For the occupation update adopted here, let T=R(I−Dε) and qn=RDεbn. Propagation in each cycle satisfies ξn+1=Tξn+qn. When the specified supply boundary makes propagation decay, the response to differences in source history from the same initial state and the stationary distribution under constant input are, respectively,

δξN=∑n=0N−1TN−1−nδqn,ξ*=(I−T)−1q.

The first expression retains the temporal order in which local actions arrive through successive stages, while the second gives the spatial accumulation of persistent action. After the field becomes stationary, source writing, background transport, and replenishment at the boundary continue. The far-field response of the three-dimensional, equally weighted, nearest-neighbor conservative exchange used here has the form 1/r, with its amplitude jointly determined by the net source output and return feedback. Actual propagation links the static profile to its build-up time.

Figure 7.1. Field formation and observation belong to the same physical process. The source, background, receiving matter, and apparatus evolve jointly. The available background states and coherent transfer affect matter through the maintenance phase and internal exchange, respectively; the two response branches in the figure belong to the same joint state and do not represent two independent dynamics. The action leaves records, and readout produces events, with the record R placed on the readout arrow; event positions and times use a common 3+1 representation.

Gravity links the available share of the background to the maintenance phase of matter. After a single physical calibration of the common strength, the external far field of a weak point source at rest, together with low-speed motion and clock rates in a slowly varying weak field, satisfies at leading order

Φ(r)=−GMsr,X¨=−∇Φ,dτloc=(1+Φ)dt.

The potential energy mΦ and kinetic energy |p|2/(2m) use the same mass coefficient, so the test mass cancels from the leading acceleration; the accumulation rate of the same phase also determines the local clock rate. Force and redshift thereby read the spatial gradient and temporal rhythm of the same background response. The same complete package reception further distinguishes single-package maintenance from three-package spatial overlap. With the stated independent two-state occupation preparation, actual parallel reception, finite-time control, and the same activity fraction as the field-free reference, A=h/h0 and Cm=A2, hence B=A/Cm=A−1. Persistent sources and transport produce further correlations, so this conditional relation is not a law for arbitrary backgrounds.

Electromagnetic storage and propagation follow from the same edge-flux and loop return. In the declared isolated upper band, actual auxiliary action gives

H2,EM=Hm+a2∑eNe2+b2∑p(I−Wp)†(I−Wp).

Its finite commutators connect source current, background change, and matter force, yielding the Maxwell response in a weak-phase long-wavelength window. Color fields retain the complete Gram operator of ordered matrix loops. Massive mediators retain their actual endpoint numerators. Pion exchange combines complete nucleon action with odd spatial arms to produce spin-, isospin-, and direction-dependent attraction and repulsion. Physical identifications are inherited, while explicit joint constructions establish the mechanisms with their parameter calibration and approximation regimes retained.

The finite light-excitation process connects source lowering, background generation, propagation, and energy balance. The conditional directional-radiation construction likewise preserves constraints and gives reciprocal absorption. The full background, however, does not contain only two modes. Connecting its new amplitude to the original material clocks and rods still requires constraint-preserving formation and readout. Relative electromagnetic-return calibration, control of persistent strong-background correlations, and this material connection delimit the present results from a more complete field theory.

Field observation continues within these same dynamics. Changes in probe motion, phase, and clock rate leave distinguishable records through the apparatus; the joint final state Ωout, including the detection process, and the pointer projection Πr give the event probability

pr=Tr[(I⊗Πr)Ωout].

While transferring energy and momentum, light connects distant signals and clock comparisons; an interferometer converts phase differences into outcome probabilities, and local absorption converts energy exchange into counts. Event positions and times are represented using a common three-dimensional space and one-dimensional time. When statistical readings are stable, spatial variations are smooth, and correlation contributions are controlled, these responses support a continuum field description. Matter produces fields and manifests their action within the same evolution, giving field quantities and their observation a common dynamical origin.
